source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026-11) Resilience engineering
finding: The field studies how complex adaptive systems cope with surprise. Accidents are not blamed on human error. People face goal conflicts and finite resources and trade off under time pressure. Hollnagel lists four potentials: respond, monitor, learn, anticipate. Woods lists three failure patterns: decompensation, working at cross purposes, stuck in outdated behaviour.
numbers: First symposium Oct 2004, Soderkoping, Sweden, 14 researchers. Second Nov 2006, Sophia Antipolis, 80 participants. No study statistics on the page.
limits: Tertiary source. The page gives no outcome data. Its text names two Woods concepts (graceful extensibility, sustained adaptability) though the cited paper names four.
agent_relevance: Confirms the vocabulary the schema borrows. The field is mostly case study and theory, so any rule taken from it is a design choice [D], not an effect with a size.

source: Woods (2019) Outmaneuvering complexity in worlds of surprise (Carderock lecture slides)
finding: Woods defines the three patterns of adaptive breakdown. Stuck in outdated models: the world changes but the system stays in strategies that used to be adaptive. Working at cross purposes: behaviour that is locally adaptive but globally maladaptive, from failure to coordinate across roles, units and echelons. Decompensation: capacity to adapt is exhausted as challenges cascade faster than responses can be decided and deployed.
numbers: 3 patterns. Illustrated with NASA failure history (1999: 3 space exploration failures; 2003 Columbia) and urban firefighting critical incidents.
quote: Decompensation: exhausting capacity to adapt as disturbances/challenges cascade.
limits: Slides, not a peer-reviewed paper. Evidence is qualitative case patterns. No rates or counts of how often each pattern occurs.
agent_relevance: Gives crisp operational definitions we can turn into detectors: cascade faster than response (decompensation), sub-goal wins that hurt the main goal (cross purposes), repeating a strategy after the world changed (stuck).

source: Woods (2019) Outmaneuvering complexity in worlds of surprise (Carderock lecture slides)
finding: Adaptive capacity is the potential to adjust activity patterns to handle future changes, so it exists before the disruption. It has a range with a boundary. Saturation is exhausting that range as demand rises. Risk of saturation is the inverse of the remaining range, given ongoing and upcoming demands. Capacity for manoeuvre is the quantity to protect.
numbers: No numbers. Definitions only.
quote: Risk of saturation: Inverse of remaining range or capacity for maneuver given ongoing and upcoming demands.
limits: Not an operational formula. Woods gives no unit of measure for capacity for manoeuvre.
agent_relevance: Maps to a budget view: tokens, attempts, and distinct strategies left. A saturation signal can be a count of remaining untried operators relative to open problems.

source: Woods (2019) Outmaneuvering complexity in worlds of surprise (Carderock lecture slides)
finding: Woods claims systems are brittle, not people erratic. SNAFU is the natural state because resources are finite and change is constant. People act as hidden SNAFU catchers and supply extra adaptive capacity. Optimising for known conditions raises brittleness (robust yet fragile, Carlson and Doyle). Adaptive behaviour is hijacked: new capability is used by others in ways that create new congestion, conflict and cascade.
numbers: No numbers. Cites Carlson and Doyle (2000): systems robust to designed perturbations yet fragile to unexpected ones. Cases: high-frequency trading, exchange outage 27 Apr 2018, NASA faster-better-cheaper.
quote: Failure is due to brittle systems, not erratic people.
limits: Strong claims built on selected stories (natural laboratories). No test against base rates of non-failure. Selection bias is a known risk in the field.
agent_relevance: Warns that tuning the scaffold hard to the benchmark makes it brittle off-benchmark. Matches G3 (a pass must be on something the answer was not fitted to).

source: Woods (2018) The theory of graceful extensibility: basic rules that govern adaptive systems (as described in Moerman et al. 2022 and in Woods slides)
finding: Graceful extensibility is the ability of a system to extend its capacity to adapt when surprise challenges its boundaries. It is stated as 10 proto-theorems in 3 subsets: A (S1-S3) managing risk of saturation, B (S4-S6) networks of adaptive units, C (S7-S10) outmanoeuvring constraints (perspective bounds, mis-calibration). It follows from two assumptions: finite resources and continuing change.
numbers: 10 proto-theorems, 3 subsets. S1 all units have bounds. S2 events occur outside the bounds. S3 units must modify and extend capacity. S4 no single unit is enough alone. S5 neighbours can monitor and shift each other's capacity. S6 others' goals change your pressures. S7 behaviour near saturation differs from far from it. S8 all units are local. S9 perspective is bounded. S10 mis-calibration is the norm.
limits: I read the theory only through a secondary paper and the author's slides; the 2018 paper is paywalled. The theory is verbal, not mathematical. Woods calls them proto-theorems.
agent_relevance: S7 and S10 are the useful ones for one agent: it behaves differently near its limit, and it mis-estimates its own limit. Supports an externally counted budget and a checked self-estimate.

source: Moerman, Pilot, Kroes et al. (2022) Graceful extensibility in asset management: extending the capacity to adapt in managing cyber-physical railway systems. Cogn Tech Work 24:21-38
finding: First empirical test of the proto-theorems. A single case study of the Dutch-Belgian V250 train introduction (services cancelled after 2 months of operation). Pattern matching against 24 sub-patterns of the 10 proto-theorems. The majority matched.
numbers: 21 of 24 sub-patterns matched; 3 not fully observed. Share of coded items: subset A 31%, subset B 46%, subset C 23%. S1 and S8 each only 2% of coded items; S6 highest at 18%. The case gave no evidence for the distinction between base and extended adaptive capacity (S7.1).
limits: One case, one coder, no independent second coder, so confirmation bias is possible. Case chosen as a failure. Single theory only; rival theories not tested. Authors call it a first attempt.
agent_relevance: The only quantified test of the theory found, and it is weak (21 of 24 match in one case). Treat the theory as a source of hypotheses [S], not as established.

source: Moerman et al. (2022) Graceful extensibility in asset management
finding: In the V250 case the system turned brittle and broke down when stakeholders were not willing to extend capacity for manoeuvre (for example by repairing trains). Trial operations could not simulate commercial operation. Authors argue that excess control creates an illusion of control that stops people looking for spare capacity.
numbers: Failures on another train (TRAXX Amsterdam-Breda, April 2011) emerged only after one week of operation.
limits: Qualitative, single case. Reasons are the authors' interpretation.
agent_relevance: Supports a hard rule that a plan or test pass is not proof of readiness (G3). Reserve capacity should be kept, not spent on the first plan.

source: David and Schraagen (2018) Analysing communication dynamics at the transaction level: the case of Air France Flight 447. Cogn Tech Work 20:637-649
finding: Applied a relational event model to the AF447 cockpit voice transcript. After the autopilot disconnected, the pilots' communication shifted: they dropped institutional patterns, relied more on the immediately preceding message (recency, persistence) and on local rules, and reached for partners they had talked to less. This is a measured instance of loss of coordination in an unexpected situation.
numbers: Two phases: normal and emergency (02:08:19 to 02:14:26.9). Only 3 agents. Normal phase: 10% of events with 3 people in the cockpit, 90% with 2. Emergency: 61% with 3, 38% with 2. Event counts about 268 (normal) and 177 (emergency) as read from a garbled table. Models compared by BIC against a null model.
limits: The authors call it preliminary: tiny group (3), one incident, a 2-hour recorder, transcript coding by few raters. Many effects were weak or non-significant. Table text was garbled when extracted, so counts are approximate.
agent_relevance: A concrete, countable signature of working at cross purposes and loss of structure under surprise. A multi-step agent could log whether its steps start depending only on the previous step (recency) rather than on the plan.

source: Cook and Rasmussen (2005) Going solid: a model of system dynamics and consequences for patient safety. Qual Saf Health Care 14:130-134
finding: Safety is dynamic, not a fixed property. Hospitals were loosely coupled and so absorbed surges. Efficiency drives removed the buffers, so one area can come to depend on small events in distant areas. This tight coupling is called going solid. The paper extends Rasmussen's dynamic safety model to explain how this leads to accidents.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract. Only the abstract was opened; the full PDF was blocked.
quote: This tight coupling condition is called "going solid".
limits: Only the abstract read. Conceptual model for hospitals, no tested prediction. Full text blocked by a bot check.
agent_relevance: A pipeline with no slack (every stage depends on the last, no spare budget) is the agent version of going solid. Keep slack: a reserve of calls and an independent check path.

source: Westrum (2004) A typology of organisational cultures. Qual Saf Health Care 13(Suppl 2):ii22-27
finding: Westrum proposes that information flow is both influential and a marker of culture, and so predicts how an organisation responds to problems. Three types: pathological, bureaucratic, generative. Support is case studies and some systematic research, and the author says the link between information culture and error reporting needs more work before it can be called definitive.
numbers: No statistics on the page I opened (abstract only).
limits: Abstract only. Typology is descriptive. Author states evidence is not definitive.
agent_relevance: For one agent the analogue is information flow between its own steps: failing outputs must reach the revision step unfiltered (G2), and bad news must not be suppressed by a judge.

source: Braithwaite, Ludlow, Churruca et al. (2024) Resilient health care performance in the real world: fixing problems that never happened. BMC Health Serv Res
finding: Synthesis of 8 earlier Resilient Health Care case studies into four themes: responsiveness, adaptiveness, local adoption of policy, interventional consequentiality. Staff adapt in ways that rules do not prescribe. The paper uses Hollnagel's watchwords respond, monitor, learn, anticipate, but not Woods's concepts.
numbers: Case figures: ED riot, 100+ patients in 4 hours (double normal rate). Blizzard, 48 home-palliative patients affected. 170 of 400 hospitals still kept concentrated KCl in patient areas. Drug process: 19 stages, 41 needs, 45 problems.
quote: strictly following safety guidelines would potentially come at the expense of patient lives
limits: Secondary synthesis, purposive inductive case selection, no quality appraisal, authors belong to the network that wrote the source chapters (advocacy risk). No outcome measures.
agent_relevance: Shows adaptive deviation from rules can be correct, a caution for rigid guardrails. Our guardrails are code-checked gates, so adaptation must come as allowed operators, not rule breaking.

source: Braithwaite et al. (2024) Resilient health care performance in the real world (simulation case, Deutsch et al.)
finding: Simulation in a new paediatric hospital improved monitoring and anticipation by finding latent safety threats before opening. Restrictive alerts produced workarounds. Teams in surgery sometimes reverted to the old method.
numbers: 37 latent safety threats found in 24 simulation sessions (8 centre-based plus 16 in situ).
limits: Counts come from one cited case; no control group. Not a test of the four potentials.
agent_relevance: Pre-deployment stress runs (like chaos tests) find latent faults. For the agent: run mutated inputs and adversarial items before trusting the scaffold.

source: Woods (2015) Four concepts for resilience and the implications for the future of resilience engineering. Reliab Eng Syst Saf 141:5-9 (as cited in Moerman 2022, David 2018, Liu 2026)
finding: Woods (2015) splits resilience into four concepts: rebound from trauma, robustness (handling anticipated disturbances), graceful extensibility (extending capacity when surprise hits the boundary), and sustained adaptability (adapting over long periods as conditions change). Brittleness is the sudden collapse when events push the system beyond its boundaries.
numbers: 4 concepts.
limits: Read through citing papers because the original is paywalled. Concepts are definitions, not measured constructs.
agent_relevance: Gives four test dimensions: recovery after error, performance on expected perturbations, behaviour at the edge of competence, and performance over a long run of changing tasks.

source: Cartography of accident causation models: remapping the modelling landscape (2025), PMC12516668
finding: Reviews 30 accident models and says labels such as linear/nonlinear and systemic are inconsistent. FRAM is classed as structural; its essential element is the textual description of functions and six properties (input, output, resource, control, precondition, time). FRAM has been criticised as impractical for complex systems. The accident pyramid assumption does not survive rigorous statistical validation.
numbers: 30 models reviewed individually. FRAM has 6 function properties. Reviews list 3, 5 or 1 systems models depending on author (Underwood and Waterson 2014; Grant et al. 2018; Leveson 2020).
quote: there has not been a single accident causation model that can explain all kinds of accidents in any given context
limits: Only about half of the 206k-character text was read; the resilience and Safety-II positioning was in the unread half.
agent_relevance: Even the best-known models give no tested prediction. Do not import FRAM as a procedure; at most borrow the six-property function template for describing a step.

source: The need for general adaptive capacity: discussing resilience with complex adaptive systems theory (2025), PMC12369295
finding: Conceptual argument that general adaptive capacity is the core of resilience. Simple and complicated systems cannot cope outside predefined load limits. Specialisation makes systems brittle, while diversity, redundancy and preparedness raise general adaptive capacity. It follows Woods in saying capacity should not be equated with resilience.
numbers: No quantitative analysis. Cites Bergstrom et al. (2009): ship crews split by experience into 3 groups; the most experienced did best overall but poorly in unexpected situations.
quote: General adaptive capacity is the core feature of resilience
limits: No data. Does not discuss graceful extensibility or the four potentials. Notes the bounce-back view is criticised.
agent_relevance: The Bergstrom result (expertise tuned to the expected hurts in the unexpected) is the human analogue of a prompt tuned to a benchmark. Keep general operators, not specialised ones.

source: Liu, Zhai, Gong et al. (2026) Resilience Matters for Embodied Agents System: New Metrics, Systematic Evaluation, and Optimization. arXiv 2608.23839
finding: Turns Woods's concepts into three metrics for LLM-driven embodied agents: Rebound (recovery cost Crec), Stability, and Graceful Extensibility (largest stress level with acceptable execution). Tested 10 agents on 400 household tasks in Habitat-Sim. Outcome success rate hides large differences in recovery process.
numbers: 400 tasks, 10 methods. Among successes, physical perturbation raised recovery cost from 11.6 to 36.3. Semantic perturbation raised instability to 0.32. Recovery cost vs perturbation intensity Spearman 0.82. Reflexion and CoPAL had near-equal success rate (56.3% vs 55.8%) but recovery cost differed 4.8 times.
limits: Preprint, one simulator, metrics defined by the authors, LLM judge used in the evaluation layer. Maps four concepts onto three metrics, dropping sustained adaptability.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that equal accuracy hides different resilience. Log recovery cost and a stress-response curve, not only pass rate, when we compare scaffolds.

source: Liu et al. (2026) Resilience Matters for Embodied Agents System (optimisation section)
finding: Resilience aspects trade off: improving graceful extensibility raised recovery cost. Metric-guided fixes helped. Feedback-guided recovery cut recovery cost and recovery window. A recent-action-history smoothing cut step-to-step instability.
numbers: Feedback-guided recovery cut Crec from 59.11 to 33.73 and the recovery window from 3.13 to 2.38. Policy-stability fix cut step instability from 0.3185 to 0.2552. Weakest-stress-capacity method (AgentEvolver) had low Crec 19.2; another had stability 0.149 but Crec 43.5.
limits: Same single benchmark and authors; improvements are self-reported on the framework they built. No independent replication.
agent_relevance: Expect trade-offs: more reserve and extensibility cost more recovery work. Pick the setting per deployment, as the paper says; do not claim a free win.

source: Owotogbe (2025) Assessing and enhancing the robustness of LLM-based multi-agent systems through chaos engineering. arXiv 2505.03096
finding: A doctoral-symposium plan, not a result. It proposes chaos engineering (injecting agent failures, delays, hallucinations) to find weak points in LLM multi-agent systems. It lists planned metrics: response time, fault detection rate, error rate, resource use. It does not cite Woods or Hollnagel and has no measured results.
numbers: No results. 3 sub-questions. Plans a multivocal literature review (under review at ACM Computing Surveys) and action research with an industry partner.
limits: No data. Chaos engineering comes from software operations, not from resilience engineering theory, even though the aim is similar.
agent_relevance: Fault injection is a practical test of the potential to respond. We can inject a wrong tool output or a mutated example and see whether G2 and G3 catch it.

source: Woods and Branlat (2011) Basic patterns in how adaptive systems fail. In Hollnagel, Paries, Woods, Wreathall (eds) Resilience Engineering in Practice, Ashgate, ch. 10
finding: The founding statement of the three patterns, drawn from fieldwork in healthcare, mission control, military operations and urban firefighting. Per search snippets: decompensation is automated compensation hiding a growing disturbance until it runs out; cross purposes is locally adaptive but globally maladaptive; stuck is failure to change routines when conditions change.
numbers: No numbers seen. Not opened (page returned 403).
limits: Not opened. Content taken from search snippets and from later citing papers, which agree with each other.
agent_relevance: Decompensation fits an agent whose repair loop masks a growing error until the budget is gone; track error growth across attempts.

source: Hollnagel (2014) Safety-I and Safety-II; Hollnagel, Paries, Woods, Wreathall (2011) Resilience Engineering in Practice
finding: Hollnagel's four potentials: respond to what happens, monitor critical developments, anticipate future threats and opportunities, learn from past events including successes. They must be seen together. A Resilience Assessment Grid gives sets of questions per potential. Safety-II asks why things go right.
numbers: 4 potentials. No effect sizes. From search snippets only.
limits: Not opened. No validation data for the grid found in this session.
agent_relevance: Maps cleanly to loop stages: monitor (checks), respond (operators), learn (carry lessons), anticipate (look ahead). But no evidence that all four are needed.

source: Woods, Hollnagel and Leveson (eds) (2006) Resilience Engineering: Concepts and Precepts. Ashgate
finding: The founding volume from the 2004 symposium. It frames safety as presence of capacity to cope, not absence of error. Known here through the Wikipedia page only.
numbers: 14 attendees at the 2004 symposium (from Wikipedia).
limits: Not opened. Edited collection of essays; no experiments.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Rasmussen (1997) Risk management in a dynamic society: a modelling problem. Safety Science 27(2-3):183-213
finding: The drift model: work practices migrate under pressure of economics, workload and effort toward the boundary of acceptable performance. Cook and Rasmussen (a09) build on it. From background knowledge, not opened.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened; reported from background knowledge.
agent_relevance: An agent under token or time pressure may drift toward skipping checks. Keep checks as code gates so they cannot drift.

source: Carlson and Doyle (2000) Highly optimized tolerance: robustness and design in complex systems. Phys Rev Lett 84:2529
finding: Cited by Woods as the formal root of robust-yet-fragile. Systems tuned for designed perturbations become fragile to unexpected ones. Seen only through the quote in Woods slides (a04).
numbers: Quote from slides: robust to perturbations they were designed to handle, yet fragile to unexpected perturbations and design flaws.
limits: Not opened. This is the closest thing to a mathematical model beneath the theory, and it is outside resilience engineering.
agent_relevance: Formal reason to expect a benchmark-tuned scaffold to fail on new tasks; test on held-out families.

source: Perrow (1984) Normal Accidents; Reason (2000); Amalberti (2001) (as cited in David and Schraagen 2018 and PMC12516668)
finding: Competing traditions the resilience papers cite: normal accident theory, high-reliability organisations, Reason's error model. The AF447 paper cites the paradox of being almost totally safe (Amalberti 2001; Reason 2000): unexpected unmodelled situations always remain. The cartography paper says NAT is pessimistic and HRO conflates safety with reliability.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Primary works not opened; only how others describe them.
agent_relevance: The almost-totally-safe paradox applies: a scaffold that handles all tested failures leaves the untested ones. Keep an impasse detector for the rest.

source: Dekker (2011) Drift into failure; Wears et al. (2008) emergency department adaptation; Bergstrom et al. (2009) ship crews (as cited in PMC12369295 and Moerman 2022)
finding: Other empirical and conceptual strands: ED adaptation to high load (Wears 2008, cited in Moerman), drift into failure (Dekker), and the ship-crew study where the most experienced group did best overall but poorly in unexpected situations (cited in a15).
numbers: Bergstrom 2009: 3 experience groups (from a15). No other numbers.
limits: Primary papers not opened.
agent_relevance: Use the ship-crew pattern as a hypothesis to test in agents: does a better-tuned scaffold lose more on surprise items?

source: Session summary: where the numbers are
finding: Across the sources opened, the quantitative base for resilience engineering is thin. There is one pattern-matching test of the theory (21 of 24 sub-patterns, one case), one transcript model (3 agents, preliminary), a case synthesis of 8 healthcare studies, and one 2026 LLM-agent metrics paper. No randomised study or replication of the four potentials was found. SUBFIELDS.md already says opened pages cite no quantitative outcome studies.
numbers: 21/24 matches; 400 tasks and 10 agents (LLM paper); 8 cases; 30 accident models.
limits: OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and arXiv APIs were rate-limited; Woods 2015, 2018 and Woods and Branlat 2011 paywalled. A gap in my search is not proof that no studies exist.
agent_relevance: Mark every rule taken from this field [S] or [D]. Do not add an operator from it without our own measurement.
